newsitem.title: EAST TIMOR: East Timor's Belo says little hope of solution.
newsitem.headline: East Timor's Belo says little hope of solution.

text.p: Nobel laureate Bishop Carlos Belo said on Thursday he was not hopeful about a new United Nations effort to resolve East Timor's future, and urged Indonesia to grant a measure of autonomy to its people.
"(For many years) I hear the same things, the same resolutions," Belo told Reuters in an interview at his home in Dili, the capital of Indonesia-ruled East Timor
"I am not hopeful," he said.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan appointed a special envoy last month to seek a solution to East Timor, a former Portuguese colony invaded by Indonesia in 1975 and annexed a year later.
Most residents of the Roman Catholic-dominated territory do not accept Indonesia's rule, but Jakarta has refused their pleas for self-determination, which have been backed by Portugal.
Residents believe 200,000 people were killed during the invasion, a subsequent famine and more than two decades of strife.
In the past 18 months, more than 100 East Timorese youths have entered embassies in Jakarta and been granted political asylum in Portugal.
The U.N. envoy, Jamsheed Marker of Pakistan, arrived in Jakarta on Thursday and was to visit East Timor on Saturday.
Belo, although he spoke cheerfully and smiled frequently, held out little hope, saying little had changed in East Timor for years.
"For me it is the same. There is no substantial chance," he said. "There are demonstrations by the young people. They arrest them and put them in detention without trial.
"This is our daily cross. Here we have (experienced) fear many times, given the number of soldiers, the number of troops (in the area)," he said.

The bishop, who was jointly awarded the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize along with Jose Ramos-Horta, a self-exiled spokesman for East Timorese self-determination, said some autonomy from Jakarta was essential in any solution.
"Timor is different culturally, historically from other parts of Indonesia," he said. "Give some concession, let the people have their autonomy."
He said winning the Nobel prize had put the international spotlight on East Timor but had little other effects.
"Now everybody knows there is East Timor. But how you treat and fulfill the aspirations of the people and also hopes of the Nobel Committee is still to come," he said.
The Nobel Peace Prize Committee said last year that the 1996 award was given to Belo and Ramos-Horta in the hope that a just solution to the problem of East Timor would be found.
"There should be a solution," Belo said.

"But the solution...should be internationally accepted and recognised. The people of East Timor like to maintain their identity...whether social, religious or cultural. They like their identity to be respected. They should have more voice to take their decisions."
Belo also said he was unaware of the circumstances in which an Indonesian soldier was killed outside Dili cathedral on Christmas eve last year, but said he had learned that the man was armed.
An Australian bishop has said the man was paid to assassinate Belo and was killed by the bishop's supporters.
The Indonesian military has said he was off-duty and had gone to the cathedral as a worshipper on his own accord.
"I don't agree with this radical action of killing that man," Belo said. "But the problem is that he was there. He had a gun."
